column146: She is a 66-year-old right-handed woman with a history of epilepsy and a right amygdala/hippocampus laser ablation.  An EMU admission captured no seizures, noting rare right temporal sharp waves/transients, and right temporal slowing.  However, a more recent EMU admission captured 5 seizures (4 typical FAS and 1 subclinical seizure), all arising from the right temporal region.  Her medications at the time testing included eslicarbazepine acetate (Aptiom), topirimate (Topamax), and cenobamate (Xcopri). Updated imaging was ordered but not completed at the time of this evaluation.     The patient's overall IQ continues to be in the Average Range, with commensurate verbal and visual perceptual skills.  Her attention/working memory were slightly variable, but generally intact for verbal and non-verbal stimuli.  Her performance was also variable on tests of learning/memory with no specific pattern in terms of non-verbal compared to verbal information.  She performed well on most tests of executive functioning, except for impaired novel problem solving and semantic verbal fluency.  Her performance continues to be weak/ impaired on tests of visual-spatial perception (line orientation, and visual puzzles) and constructional skills.  Despite wearing hearing aids, she occasionally had difficulty with test directions, but her basic language functions were intact.  Fine motor speed/dexterity continues to be significantly slower for her non-dominant left hand.  She is currently not reporting significant symptoms of either depression or anxiety (minimal range).       Taken together, her test pattern continues to show specific impairments on tasks typically mediated by the right hemisphere, specifically visual-spatial perception and constructional skills.  In addition, she continues to be significantly slower with her non-dominant left hand on a task of fine motor speed/dexterity. These findings are consistent with her history of damage due to a ruptured right posterior communicating artery aneurysm.  In terms of learning and memory, her performance was extremely variable, ranging from the Superior to the Impaired Range, and did not lateralize in terms of verbal versus non-verbal material. her performance was also impaired on two specific tests of executive functioning, novel problem solving and semantic fluency.  It is important to note that her performance was extremely variable throughout this evaluation, which was at least partly due to behavioral issues.  For example, she was often argumentative, resisted even attempting several tasks, and requested frequent/long breaks.

Visually mediated aspects of executive dysfunction and poor learning and retrieval of visual information suggest non-dominant (likely right) frontotemporal dysfunction and provide clinical correlation with seizures that appear to originate from the right anterior to mid temporal lobe, while particularly weak facial memory may localize to the inferior non-dominant temporal lobe. Weaknesses in auditory attention, working memory, and phonemic fluency may suggest more diffuse frontal involvement or the effects of her white matter abnormalities. Taken together, she meets criteria for a Mild Neurocognitive Disorder due to epilepsy. Her visual memory performance, although weaker than verbal memory, generally improved with recognition formats (with the exception of facial recognition), suggesting a retrieval deficit as opposed to impaired retention, arguing against primary non-dominant mesial temporal dysfunction. The asymmetry in memory provides a reasonable lateralization or bias in deficits to the non-dominant hemisphere. She reports word finding problems; thus, it should be noted that she shows mixed results with fluency in our data, nothing at the level of an aphasia, but more unstructured word retrieval demands are harder for her.
